name: Caesarism
summary: Caesarism is personal, plebiscitary rule in which one commanding figure, usually with army backing, claims to stand above warring classes and parties and to resolve a crisis that ordinary politics cannot. Legitimacy comes from popular acclaim rather than from parliament, and the leader's power is not checked by independent institutions. In Gramsci's account it arises when opposed social forces balance each other in a catastrophic stalemate, and may be progressive or reactionary depending on whom the arbiter helps.
scope: The classical concept as developed from Romieu's 1850 polemic and the Napoleonic regimes (Napoleon I, Napoleon III's social Caesarism), through Weber's account of plebiscitary mass democracy and Gramsci's Prison Notebooks analysis, with Mussolini and Vallenilla Lanz as later adopters. Excludes the loose modern use of the word for any populist strongman. Napoleon III's regime is the best-documented case, so many answers lean on it; it overlaps heavily with the separate Bonapartism audit. No Caesarist writer produced a full programme, so most answers on economics and social issues are low-confidence inferences.

keyFigures.name: Napoleon III
keyFigures.role: Ruler whose plebiscitary Second Empire is the standard historical case of social Caesarism.

keyFigures.name: Antonio Gramsci
keyFigures.role: Marxist theorist who developed the analytic concept of Caesarism as arbitration in a catastrophic equilibrium of forces.

keyFigures.name: Max Weber
keyFigures.role: Sociologist who argued that mass democracy tends toward Caesarist plebiscitary leadership.

sources.title: Selections from the Prison Notebooks, 'Caesarism' (trans. Hoare and Nowell Smith)

sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Practice of Caesarist rule: plebiscites, weak legislature, press control, 1851 coup arrests, state-led economy, free-trade treaty, Church relations, foreign policy.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Caesarist rule has no health doctrine; Napoleon III's social Caesarism paired authority with worker-oriented measures, but nothing commits it to universal state care.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: No wage-setting doctrine; social Caesarism courted workers with welfare gestures while an arbiter above classes avoids siding firmly with either wage side.

public-ownership.rationale: Caesarist regimes used state initiative in infrastructure without a doctrine of public ownership; adherents range from state builders to friends of capital.

property-fundamental.rationale: Gramsci's reactionary Caesarism protects the propertied bloc and progressive Caesarism may override it, so the arbiter treats property as a means of order, not a sacred right.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: No doctrine on speech content; the regime restricts opposition speech but not for hate-speech reasons.

strong-leader.rationale: The core of the ideology: a great personality entrusted with arbitrating a deadlocked situation, as Caesar and Napoleon did.

state-harmful.rationale: Caesarism exists to rescue and rebuild the state through a single arbiter; anarchist rejection of the state is the opposite of its premise.

limit-guns.rationale: No doctrine on civilian firearms; a regime monopolising force might restrict them, but adherents are not committed.

empower-police-military.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is not about military spending, which this statement now asks about alone.

reviewHistory.rationale: Gramsci notes that the military was decisive in bringing earlier Caesarist solutions about, and Caesarism ties rule to the army and police.
reviewHistory.author: claude-sonnet-5-5

reviewHistory.rationale: Nulled (statement review, 2026-11-11): its rationale is not about military spending, which this statement now asks about alone.
reviewHistory.author: claude-opus-5-5

decide-locally.rationale: Weber's marks of Caesarism include refusing autonomous powers within government, so decisions concentrate in the centre.

more-religion-public.rationale: Bohmer's early usage framed Caesarism as the state subordinating the Church, while Napoleon III backed the Church; adherents split.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Caesarist leaders typically appeal to national unity and rebirth in the name of the people, so culture and tradition serve legitimacy.

reduce-immigration.rationale: No stated immigration doctrine; adherents differ by case.

free-trade.rationale: Napoleon III signed the Cobden-Chevalier free-trade treaty yet other Caesarist regimes were protectionist; no consistent doctrine.

nation-first.rationale: Caesarist rhetoric centres on national unity and glory, and Mussolini and Napoleon III pursued national interest abroad.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: Napoleon III intervened abroad for prestige and sometimes liberal-national causes, but humanitarian grounds are not doctrine.

limit-growth.rationale: Caesarist regimes pride themselves on material progress and grand public works, as under the Second Empire.

revolution-justified.rationale: Caesarism arises to close a revolutionary-reactionary stalemate, with progressive Caesarism allowed as a managed substitute for revolution; it opposes revolutionary overthrow.

experts-over-public.rationale: Caesarists claim to speak for the people against elites and experts alike; no firm view.

central-planning.rationale: The Second Empire directed development without running industry; full planning is not part of the tradition.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Policy varied by regime, with Napoleon III cutting tariffs while others protected; no stated rule.

state-directs-investment.rationale: The Second Empire government actively built railways, ports and banks to promote growth, the model of social Caesarism.

widespread-small-property.rationale: Napoleonic regimes relied on the peasant smallholder base for support, but Caesarism has no property doctrine.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: Caesarism arbitrates within existing class society and keeps it; abolishing wage labour is revolutionary aim.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: Mussolini's Italy adopted corporatism, but Caesarism as a whole has no required labour-relations system.

one-party-rule.rationale: Mussolini built a party state, but Napoleon and Napoleon III ruled through plebiscite and personal power; adherents split.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Caesarism claims popular rather than hereditary legitimacy, though Napoleon III founded a dynasty; split.

democracy-best.rationale: Weber has mass democracy tending toward Caesarism and Spengler sees Caesarism succeeding democracy; adherents prize acclaimed leadership over elected, accountable government.

direct-votes.rationale: Plebiscitary acclaim is a defining feature, as Napoleon's referendums showed, though citizens vote on leaders and regimes more than on laws.

workers-councils.rationale: Caesarism concentrates power in one arbiter; council power would be exactly the class-led alternative it prevents.

right-to-secede.rationale: Intolerance of independent power centres and national unity rhetoric rule out regional secession.

natural-rulers.rationale: The doctrine rests on the exceptional great personality who can arbitrate where others cannot.

political-violence-never.rationale: Napoleon III's 1851 coup arrested thousands and Gramsci notes military coups as the usual route to Caesarism.

war-builds-character.rationale: Caesarist leaders often won legitimacy by conquest, but glorifying war as character-building is not core doctrine.

separate-church-state.rationale: Early usage stressed state mastery over church while Napoleon III courted it; adherents ranged both ways.

private-courts-defense.rationale: A regime that concentrates force and tolerates no autonomous power would not privatise courts or defense.

military-superiority.rationale: Caesarist rule leans on the army and wins prestige through military strength.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Classical Caesarism appeals to the people or nation as a political unit; ethnic definition is not core.

class-struggle-history.rationale: Gramsci treats Caesarism as arising from class conflict, but Caesarists themselves present the leader as above classes.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Social Caesarism offers material improvement but within hierarchy; equal outcomes are not its goal.

colonial-reparations.rationale: Caesarist regimes pursued colonial expansion, as Napoleon III roughly doubled French colonial territory.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Napoleonic regimes celebrated industrial progress, railways and urban modernisation.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Modernising, but disruption of existing institutions is not what an order-seeking arbiter wants.

algorithmic-government.rationale: The doctrine centres on a personal leader, not algorithmic decision-making.

restore-past-order.rationale: Caesarism is forward-looking in its progressive form and conservative in its reactionary form, so adherents are split.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Caesarist rule justifies itself by resolving crisis and delivering order, and Gramsci notes the formula is judged by what the intervention achieves.

means-match-ends.rationale: Caesarism accepts coups and force to reach order.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Wholly foreign to a state-building tradition.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Caesarism preserves class society and its economic order.

production-for-use.rationale: A socialist aim that Caesarism, as arbiter within class society, does not hold.

profit-exploitation.rationale: Caesarism mediates between classes rather than endorsing exploitation theory.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Caesarism is rule by an arbiter above classes, not a class dictatorship.

collective-farming.rationale: Napoleonic regimes drew on smallholding peasantry; no collectivism.

taxation-theft.rationale: The state-building regime taxed to fund railways, army and public works.

harm-principle.rationale: Weber's Caesarism tolerates no autonomous power, and its regimes censor press and opposition for order.

conscription.rationale: Rule resting on the army and national prestige favours conscription, as under both Napoleons.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Caesarism builds legitimacy on acclamation and the vote, not exit.

state-as-business.rationale: It is personal rule claiming national mission, not customer-service management.

positive-liberty.rationale: Social Caesarism offered material welfare for the masses, but the doctrine has no theory of freedom.

media-academia-power.rationale: Caesarist populism attacks establishment elites, but media power is not a core claim.

organic-representation.rationale: Mussolini used corporate representation but Caesarism does not require it.

national-rebirth.rationale: Caesarist leaders often appeal to national unity and rebirth in the name of an abstract people.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Napoleon I and III expanded territory and colonies for prestige, as Caesar did in Gaul.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Caesarism rests on acclaim and personal following more than feudal oaths, though army loyalty to the commander matters; split.

bound-labor.rationale: Napoleonic regimes were post-revolutionary and abolished feudal labour obligations.

economic-freedom.rationale: Caesarism holds that political order and the leader come first; Weber's Caesarism is intolerant of independent power centres.

rule-by-example.rationale: Caesarism rules through acclaim, army and law-making power, not moral example alone.

national-self-determination.rationale: Napoleon III backed Italian unification and national causes, and Caesarism glorifies the nation.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Never addressed in the sources; a disciplined, order-minded regime might favour it, but adherents have no stated view.

class-collaboration.rationale: The arbiter stops mutually destructive class conflict and freezes antagonism, so reconciliation of classes under the leader is central.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Napoleonic regimes celebrated national heritage and monuments.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: No doctrine; historic regimes were conventional but Caesarism does not require it.

ban-interest.rationale: The Second Empire promoted investment banks and credit.

state-class-instrument.rationale: Gramsci sees Caesarism as an arbiter with relative autonomy, though it still serves one bloc in reactionary form; adherents say it stands above classes.

elite-replacement.rationale: Conspiracy view not found in Caesarist sources.

proportional-representation.rationale: Disdain for parliament and fragmented parties means a strongman rejects proportional bargaining; Gramsci notes coalitions are a first stage of Caesarism, though.

national-mission.rationale: Caesarist leaders often claim national greatness or mission, but not as a doctrine of spreading governance.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Structural-patriarchy analysis is a modern feminist claim with no Caesarist counterpart; adherents have no common view.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Caesarist populism claims the parliamentary class is corrupt and out of touch with the people.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: A regime resting on the army and refusing independent powers will not hold its security forces accountable.

night-watchman-state.rationale: The arbiter state is strong and interventionist.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Napoleonic regimes kept equality before the civil code but denied political equality; Mussolini rejected equality; split.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: The Napoleonic Civil Code applied a single civil law, a core model for Caesarist centralisation.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Conversion law is not a Caesarist concern, and historic regimes like the Second Empire had no conversion restrictions to speak of.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Napoleon III backed church schooling while Bohmer's usage envisioned state mastery; split.

state-strengthens-encirclement.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist state theory; Caesarism neither adopts nor addresses it, though it favours a strong state anyway.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Caesarism rests on plebiscitary acclamation, claiming popular consent without independent checks.

trade-surplus.rationale: Caesarist regimes differ on trade policy, from Napoleon III's free-trade treaties to protectionist strongmen, so there is no common doctrine on running surpluses.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Napoleon III seized power by force in the 1851 coup, and Gramsci describes coups as the usual route to Caesarism.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: The Second Empire banned and suppressed opposition parties.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Rule by one arbiter with no independent counter-power is what republicans call domination.

separated-powers.rationale: Weber's marks of Caesarism include disdain for parliament and non-toleration of autonomous powers; the regime concentrates power in one person.

vanguard-party.rationale: Caesarism relies on one personality and the people, not a disciplined revolutionary party.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Social Caesarism courted the poor but did not make them first priority.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: Caesarism puts power in a chosen leader, not randomly chosen officials.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Napoleon III's coup was followed by roughly 26,000 arrests and press controls justified as defending order.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Neither Weber nor Gramsci nor the Second Empire record supply a doctrine on price caps; a crisis-managing arbiter might use them.

party-controls-media.rationale: The Second Empire required government permission for political newspapers, and Weber's Caesarism has disdain for independent powers.

party-commands-army.rationale: Caesarism usually puts the army under the leader rather than any party.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: The Second Empire paid its officials and notables well and kept a hierarchical state; levelling pay is not a Caesarist aim.

head-commands-forces.rationale: The 1852 constitution gave the head of state authority to declare war, sign treaties and command; the strongman leads the army.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Church governance is not a Caesarist issue; Napoleon III supported the Church but left internal governance alone.

clerical-rule.rationale: Caesarism puts power in the leader, not clergy.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Caesarism rejects the stance as treason against the national arbiter.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: Regimes censored the press for order, but moral art censorship is not doctrinal.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Barred from a second term, Louis-Napoléon seized power in 1851 and had plebiscites extend and then make permanent his rule, the pattern of the first Napoleon's consulate for life; Caesarism rejects limits on the plebiscitary leader's tenure.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Napoleon III built alliances with Britain and Italy; no isolationist doctrine.

people-in-arms.rationale: Caesarism rests on a professional army loyal to the leader.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: Cultural-relativist equality is not a Caesarist claim, though national-pride rhetoric points the other way, so adherents are split.

death-penalty.rationale: Order-focused regimes hold harsh penalties, but unspecified.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Not a Caesarist issue, and the Napoleonic regimes had no stance on teaching evolution.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Not part of the doctrine; regimes that censored the press for order might restrict it, but adherents have no shared view.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: The Napoleonic Civil Code leaned on descent, but Caesarism as a doctrine has no stated rule, so it is left open.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: No doctrine; inference from order and conformity.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: Poor-country debt relief is a modern question the tradition never addressed.

constituent-assembly.rationale: Napoleon's regimes were framed by constitutions drafted by the executive and ratified by plebiscite, bypassing assemblies.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: The Second Empire curbed press and opposition while pursuing railways, banking and rapid growth, and presented order as the condition of progress.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Weber says mass democracy tends toward Caesarism through plebiscitary elections, pure caesarist acclamation, as in the U.S. presidency.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Territorial compromise depends on the case; Napoleon III annexed and exchanged territory pragmatically, so no common line exists.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Property may be bent to the arbiter's solution, but this is not doctrinal.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Napoleon III annexed Savoy and Nice by plebiscite; Caesarism has no consistent stance.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Bohmer first used the term for the state subordinating the Church, yet Napoleon III supported it; adherents are split.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: A regime that tolerates no autonomous powers would use force against secession.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Centralisation excludes regional systems of law.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Caesarism rests on acclaim and personal achievement, not divine descent, though leader cults may form.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Tax design is not a Caesarist subject, and the arbiter's stance between classes does not settle flat versus progressive rates.

character-from-environment.rationale: Caesarism stresses the exceptional personality but has no theory of how ordinary character forms, so adherents have no shared view.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Weber stresses the rule of the plebiscitary leader unbound by parliament, and Napoleon III held broad prerogative.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Caesarism concentrates authority, though Weber wanted parliament to keep a check; Caesarists reject the mix.

leader-cult.rationale: The ideology exalts a heroic personality, and Mussolini's Italy built a personal cult.

equal-parenting.rationale: Family-court presumptions are a modern issue that Caesarist sources never touch.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: A debate internal to Marxism-Leninism, which Caesarism does not join.

land-redistribution.rationale: Napoleonic regimes relied on the existing smallholder base and kept property.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Napoleon III backed national unification and annexed Savoy; no stable rule.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Pan-ethnic union is not a Caesarist aim, though some strongmen pursued it for prestige, so adherents are split.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Gramsci's analysis is class-based, but Caesarists credit great personalities; split.

ban-cartels.rationale: Competition law is not a Caesarist issue; the Second Empire encouraged large banks and companies, but no rule follows.

no-bailouts.rationale: Caesarism has no bailout doctrine; a state-directing arbiter might rescue firms, but adherents are not committed.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Plebiscitary acclaim claims popular will over independent institutions, as Weber notes the intolerance of autonomous powers.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Napoleonic regimes created new titles and nobility while ending feudal privileges; split.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Imperial prestige drives historic Caesarist regimes.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Caesarism resists entrenched limits on the leader; Weber describes disdain for independent checks.

elective-rulers.rationale: The ruler is chosen by acclamation but then holds power, so the election logic is plebiscite rather than the political nation's choice; split.

minority-veto.rationale: Caesarism rejects veto power and powers independent of the leader.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Caesarism does not accept a right to remove the leader.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Weber lists disdain for parliament as a mark of Caesarism, and the Second Empire reduced the Assembly's authority.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Caesarism builds on mass participation through acclaim.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Gramsci's wider writing is critical of culture as a tool of order, but Caesarists themselves do not make the claim, so adherents are split.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: Gramsci's hegemony concept describes the crisis that gives rise to Caesarism, but adherents themselves do not make this claim.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Mussolini and Italian fascism embraced Caesarism, and the leader tradition conflicts with anti-fascism as a founding rule.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Caesarism's own heirs include Italian fascism and also the plebiscitary regimes of Napoleon, so adherents have no consistent view of the comparison.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Vallenilla Lanz defended a democratic Caesarism suited to Venezuelan society, an argument that institutions fit local conditions.

military-guardian-role.rationale: Gramsci says the military was decisive in making Caesarism, and the leader typically arises from the army as guardian of order.

office-by-exam.rationale: Napoleonic bureaucracy rewarded talent but Caesarism has no doctrine.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Caesarism rejects mandates binding the leader.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Pension design is not a Caesarist subject and no principle settles it.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Napoleonic regimes rested on secure private smallholding after the Revolution, so land held only for use is foreign to them.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: The 1852 constitution kept the Assembly weak on budget control, and Weber notes disdain for parliament.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Land-ownership rules for foreigners are not part of the doctrine, so adherents are split.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Second Empire prosperity celebrated material gain.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Napoleon III backed nationalist causes abroad on occasion, but arming insurgents is not a doctrine.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Caesarist great-power rulers intervened abroad for prestige, but a bloc-discipline doctrine is not part of the ideology.

job-guarantee.rationale: Napoleon III's public works programmes provided jobs, but no guarantee doctrine.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Caesarism demands obedience to the leader and the order he imposes.

non-intervention.rationale: Napoleon III intervened in Rome, Italy, Crimea and Mexico, so a ban on intervention contradicts the tradition.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Caesarist regimes controlled information and refused independent publicity.

informal-organisation.rationale: Caesarism relies on a central leader and mass acclamation.

religious-nation.rationale: Caesarism defines the nation through the leader and people, not religion.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Caesarism has no property doctrine; Gramsci's arbiter may favour either side.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Gramsci describes Caesarism as arbitration above two opposed social forces, which sits between the poles but is not a worked-out third economic course.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Weber's marks of Caesarism include intolerance of autonomous power, and Napoleon III controlled the press and arrested opponents in 1851.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Weber's Caesarism has the people acclaim a leader in plebiscites and disdains parliament, so ordinary people are acclaiming voters, not direct decision-makers.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Weber's Caesarism grounds legitimacy in popular acclaim rather than any higher source, though Napoleon III still invoked Providence in rhetoric.

ban-nda-harassment.rationale: No Caesarist doctrine on employment law; Napoleon III's social Caesarism did combine order with workers' measures, but nothing addresses this.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Gramsci stresses the army's decisive role in Caesarist solutions, and Napoleon III's rule depended on it.

rich-first.rationale: Napoleon III's economy favoured investors and state-sponsored growth but the doctrine has no stance on regional unevenness.

property-franchise.rationale: Napoleon III restored universal male suffrage and ruled through plebiscites, and Weber's account ties Caesarism to mass acclaim, which a wealth-limited electorate would undercut.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Napoleon III controlled the press by state licensing and warnings, so the Caesarist regime itself, not the wealthy, limits press freedom; Caesarists would not endorse the complaint as stated.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Weber's marks of Caesarism include disdain for parliament and intolerance of autonomous power, and Napoleon III governed by coup and decree, so personal discretion rather than binding standing law is typical.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Caesarism is concerned with arbitrating class conflict and has no stated doctrine on marriage; as a secular strongman model it would not restrict marriage by religion, an inference only.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: No Caesarist source addresses this; it is split.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Caesarist rule rests on army and police backing for the leader; Gramsci describes the arbiter relying on armed force.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Caesarism vests executive power in one acclaimed figure, the opposite of sharing it among communities.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: No stated view; Napoleon III's social Caesarism mixed state measures with Church charity.

term-limits.rationale: Napoleon III extended his term to ten years and then made himself emperor; plebiscitary rule works against term limits.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: No economic doctrine; the arbiter stands above classes and Napoleon III backed both capital and workers.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Caesarism is pragmatic arbitration of class stalemate, not a cosmic struggle; Napoleon III also managed church relations for expedience.

independent-unions.rationale: Napoleon III's regime and plebiscitary rule left no room for independent institutions or organised labour that checked the leader.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: Caesarism rules above classes as arbiter, not through workers' power; Napoleon III's social measures aimed at winning workers, not empowering them.

second-chamber.rationale: Plebiscitary rule bypasses parliament; Napoleon III's second chamber was a weak appointed body, and Weber saw the leader as direct from the people.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Caesarist rule concentrates power in the leader above independent bodies, the reverse of confederal local assemblies.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Napoleon III courted the Church while Caesarism has no spiritual doctrine; adherents split.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Caesarism claims to stand above classes and unite the people under one leader; racial organising is not part of it.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Napoleon and Napoleon III waged wars of expansion and prestige, so adherents would not confine force to defence.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Caesarist leaders often invoke external threats to justify crisis rule, but the concept itself carries no doctrine of foreign partition plots.

free-public-college.rationale: No Caesarist education programme exists; Napoleon III expanded schooling modestly, but nothing in the model commits it to tuition-free higher education.

arms-reduction.rationale: Gramsci stresses the army's decisive role in bringing Caesarist solutions, and Napoleon III pursued active military foreign policy, so deep arms cuts sit badly with it.

capital-controls.rationale: Social Caesarism combined state-led economic direction with a free-trade treaty under Napoleon III, so adherents point both ways.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Napoleon III legalized strikes in 1864 yet banned independent unions earlier; the pattern is mixed.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Caesarism seizes and uses the existing state in a crisis rather than smashing it, as Gramsci describes.

public-service-media.rationale: Napoleon III's regime tightly controlled the press, so independent media are not favoured.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: No Caesarist source addresses women's property rights; the Napoleonic Code era was unequal, but the doctrine itself is silent.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: No labour doctrine; Weber's account has the leader refusing autonomous power centres, while social Caesarism courted workers, so adherents are split.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: Early usage had the state subordinating the Church while Napoleon III favoured it; adherents ranged both ways.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Caesarist regimes used religion for support when useful but the theory takes no view on scripture.

indirect-election.rationale: Caesarist legitimacy comes from direct plebiscitary acclaim of the leader, bypassing intermediary bodies.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: Plebiscites are the defining Caesarist tool; Napoleon III used them, including on Nice and Savoy in 1860.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Caesarist rulers acted outside normal legal limits (Napoleon III's 1851 coup, suppression of opponents), but killing suspected drug users is not part of the doctrine and adherents would differ.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: Napoleon III backed national causes such as Italian unification, but kin-minority protection is not a defining Caesarist position, so adherents are split.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Gramsci and Weber describe Caesarism as plebiscitary rule above parties and parliament, with the leader appealing directly to the people.

former-empire-equal-treatment.rationale: Imperial prestige drives historic Caesarist regimes. (Carried over from former-empire-influence, "A country should cultivate political and cultural influence in regions once ruled by its predecessor empire.", with the value reversed, 2026-11-11.)

missingStatements.text: A leader may rule above parliament and parties as an arbiter between warring social classes.
missingStatements.rationale: Gramsci defines Caesarism as arbitration by a third force that freezes a catastrophic class stalemate, which no existing statement captures directly.

missingStatements.text: A head of state may legitimately take power by a military coup when ordinary politics is deadlocked.
missingStatements.rationale: Gramsci notes that regular military forces were decisive in bringing Caesarist solutions about by coup, and Napoleon III's 1851 coup was confirmed by plebiscite.

missingStatements.text: Elections should serve mainly to acclaim a leader rather than to choose between competing programmes.
missingStatements.rationale: Weber's mark of Caesarism is the plebiscitary character of elections, a pure form of acclamation of the leader.

notes: Gramsci's progressive Caesarism (Caesar, Napoleon I) and reactionary Caesarism (Napoleon III, Bismarck) differ on whom the arbiter helps, and economic answers would shift accordingly. Weber thought parliament should keep enough power to restrain the plebiscitary leader; Mussolini's adoption was far more totalising. Only the practical-regime and analytic strands are sourced; no source states a Caesarist programme on social or cultural questions.
